title: iPhone Duo Teardown: Korean Suppliers and Why Korea Pays ₩610,000 More
content:
Apple's first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, is reportedly built almost entirely on Korean components — display, camera, memory, and board materials all sourced from Korean suppliers. Yet it costs ₩610,000 more in Korea than in the US. Here's which Korean companies are reported to be inside, and why the pricing gap doesn't add up the way you'd expect.

PartJobSupplierEvidence
Display (inner foldable + outer cover)Folding OLED panel, both screensSamsung DisplaySole supplier, widely reported
Camera moduleDual-camera module assemblyLG Innotek
KRX: 011070		Reported 55–60% of new camera order
Memory (LPDDR5)Mobile DRAMSK Hynix & Samsung ElectronicsReported 70% of memory used
AP substrate & MLCCsChip-mounting board, current-stabilizing capacitorsSamsung Electro-Mechanics
KRX: 009150		Reported supplier
HingeFolding mechanismNot disclosedAmphenol, Painem Tech named as candidates; unconfirmed

1. Display — Samsung Display

A foldable phone lives or dies on how long the fold itself holds up. Both the inner folding panel and the outer cover display on the iPhone Duo are reported to come solely from Samsung Display. For Apple's first foldable, that's less a preference than a constraint — Samsung Display is widely considered the only supplier with folding-panel durability proven at this scale.

2. Camera module — LG Innotek

LG Innotek reportedly won 55–60% of the order for the new camera modules, supplying the dual-camera assembly as a complete unit rather than individual parts. It tracks with a broader trend of LG Innotek's share of Apple's camera supply chain growing year over year.

3. Memory — SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics

70% of the LPDDR5 mobile DRAM in this phone is reported to be Korean-made, split between SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. That split roughly mirrors the two companies' combined share of the global mobile DRAM market.

4. AP substrate and MLCCs — Samsung Electro-Mechanics

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is reported to supply both the substrate the main chip sits on and the MLCCs (multilayer ceramic capacitors) that keep current flowing evenly. Neither part is visible to a user, but both are directly tied to whether the device runs stable without overheating.

5. Hinge — supplier undisclosed

The hinge is the other defining component of a foldable, and while stocks like Amphenol and Painem Tech have been floated as candidates, no actual supply relationship has been confirmed. No supplier has been disclosed for this part as of this writing.

So why does Korea pay more?

Comparing iPhone Duo 256GB pricing:

  • Korea: ₩3.29 million
  • US: $1,999
  • India: ₩4.21 million (Korea is not the most expensive market)

Running the same comparison for the Galaxy Z Fold8 256GB — ₩2.2781 million in Korea versus $1,899 in the US — shows a much smaller US-Korea gap for that device. In other words: in the US, the iPhone Duo costs about $100 more than the Z Fold8. In Korea, the gap between the two phones balloons to roughly ₩1.01 million. Most of the components are made in Korea, but Korean buyers are the ones absorbing the bigger price premium.

Summary

  • Display: Samsung Display
  • Camera module: LG Innotek (55–60% share)
  • Memory: SK Hynix & Samsung Electronics (70% of LPDDR5)
  • AP substrate & MLCCs: Samsung Electro-Mechanics
  • Hinge: Supplier not disclosed

Quick FAQ

Is this officially confirmed by Apple or the suppliers?
No. The Samsung Display, LG Innotek, SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Samsung Electro-Mechanics sourcing is based on industry reporting, not an official disclosure from Apple or the companies themselves. The hinge supplier remains undisclosed entirely.

Is Korea the most expensive market for this phone?
No. India (₩4.21 million) is priced higher than Korea (₩3.29 million). The notable point is how much wider the Korea-US price gap is for the iPhone Duo compared to the Galaxy Z Fold8.

Are these suppliers Korea-listed?
LG Innotek (011070), Samsung Electro-Mechanics (009150), Samsung Electronics, and SK Hynix all trade on the KOSPI. Samsung Display is a Samsung Electronics subsidiary and is not separately listed.

Companies named are reported or disclosed suppliers; parts with no confirmed supplier are labeled as such. Images are reconstructions based on public information, not an actual physical teardown.
